meta.question: Why does our checkout use an event-driven saga instead of one database transaction?
meta.title: Checkout architecture: saga vs single transaction
meta.author: Platform team

answer.headline: Because payment, inventory and the ledger live in different systems, no single transaction can span them; a saga keeps each step reliable and undoable instead.
answer.text: A checkout touches an external payment provider, our own services and a distributed ledger. A **saga** runs these as a sequence of local steps, each with a *compensating* step that reverses it if a later step fails.
points: No two-phase commit across Stripe, Kafka and CockroachDB
A failure rolls back cleanly instead of leaving half an order
Each service scales and deploys on its own

blocks.title: Where the saga runs
blocks.caption: The Order Orchestration Engine (Temporal) coordinates every step of the checkout.

items.title: Authorise
items.text: The gateway validates the token with the auth broker.

items.title: Start the saga
items.text: The orchestrator records the order and starts the workflow.

items.title: Capture payment
items.text: Two-phase capture with the payment provider.

items.title: Commit
items.text: The ledger row is written and `OrderCreated` is published.

blocks.label: When a step fails
blocks.body:
The orchestrator runs the compensations in reverse order:

- release the payment hold
- mark the order as cancelled
- publish `OrderCancelled` so downstream systems catch up

options.name: Single database transaction
options.summary: Wrap everything in one ACID transaction.
cons: Impossible across an external payment API
Locks rows for the whole checkout
options.verdict: Not possible with an external provider.

options.name: Two-phase commit
options.summary: A coordinator asks every system to prepare, then commit.
pros: Atomic across systems that support it
cons: Stripe and Kafka do not take part in 2PC

options.name: Orchestrated saga
options.summary: Local steps with compensations, run by Temporal.
cons: Eventually consistent for a few hundred milliseconds
